title: Corporate Social Responsibility and Firms Value of Non-Financial Listed Firms Listed in Nigeria
summary: This study assessed the effect of Corporate Social Responsibility on Firms Value of listed non-financial firms in Nigeria using ICT, Oil and Gas firms as evidence of study for a ten-year period spanning from 2013 to 2024. The specific objectives of this study are to determine the effect of corporate social responsibility on share price, price earnings, market capitalization of quoted ICT, Oil and Gas firms in Nigeria. Ex-post facto research design was employed. The population of this study consist of 29 (Twenty-nine) ICT, Oil and Gas firms quoted on the Nigeria Exchange Group as at 2024, out of which ten (10) of the ICT, Oil and Gas firms were selected using purposive sampling. Secondary data were extracted from annual reports and financial statements gotten from the Nigeria Exchange Group (NGX). The study employed descriptive statistics and inferential statistics using Pearson correlation, Panel pooled Least Square (PLS) regression analysis, normality test for the study. Findings from the empirical analysis showed that CSR (β1= 0.043135; p- value of 0.0125) has a significant and positive effect on share price, CSR (β2= -0.212415; p- value of 0.0000) has a significant and positive effect on price to earnings ratio; also CSR (β3= 0.124806; p- value of 0.0001) has a non-significant and negative effect on Market Capitalization of quoted listed ICT, Oil and Gas Firms in Nigeria at 5% level of significance. Conclusively, Government should establish standard corporate social responsibility policies and encourage firms on its realization and enforcement of laws on firms that fail to adhere to its implementation. Firms should also engage in corporate social responsibility activities that will help improve their image, goodwill and profitability. Policy makers, investors should be encouraged in promoting corporate social responsibility which will ensure competitiveness and market repositioning.

title: Lean tools and Industry 4.0 technologies: a multidimensional analysis of firm performance
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how Lean/Lean Six Sigma (LSS) tools and Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies relate to firm performance across multiple dimensions and time horizons. Prior research has focused predominantly on productivity; the authors extend this view to profitability, capital structure, financing conditions and internationalization, distinguishing between short- (2020–2022) and long-term (2012–2022) performance effects. Design/methodology/approach Using survey data from 140 industrial firms in inland Portugal, Lean/LSS and I4.0 constructs were modeled through a parcel-based measurement approach and estimated using Structural Equation Modeling with robust maximum likelihood. Performance indicators were derived from secondary accounting data, expressed as short- and long-term deltas. The structural model incorporates a theoretically grounded performance cascade linking productivity, return on assets, indebtedness, interest rate and internationalization. Findings Lean/LSS and I4.0 technologies exhibit strong complementarity, yet neither shows direct effects on short- or long-term financial performance indicators. Instead, performance evolves through a powerful internal propagation mechanism: productivity improvements drive increases in return on assets, which in turn reduce indebtedness. This cascade is significant in the short term and substantially stronger over the long term, explaining up to 91.5% of long-term return on assets variance and 62% of long-term indebtedness variance. Downstream effects on interest rate and internationalization remain non-significant. Originality/value By combining a multidimensional performance framework with explicit temporal differentiation and a performance to-performance cascade, this study clarifies how operational improvements translate, or fail to translate, into financial outcomes. Results show that the impact of Lean and I4.0 is indirect and unfolds primarily through internal financial propagation rather than direct effects on top-level accounting metrics. This contributes new empirical evidence on the temporal and structural mechanisms linking operational and digital transformation to firm performance and suggests that firms should adopt a long-term perspective, combining Lean and digital transformation initiatives while monitoring performance across multiple dimensions.

title: Board characteristics and financial misconduct
summary: This paper investigates how three features of board structure relate to financial reporting misconduct in China. The analysis covers 63,650 firm-year observations for A-share companies between 2000 and 2025 and considers the proportion of independent directors, the combination of the CEO and board-chair positions, and female representation on the board. Financial restatement serves as the observable measure of misconduct. The estimates show that CEO duality is associated with fewer restatements. Board independence also has a negative coefficient, although the association weakens and loses statistical significance when the other board attributes are included. Female board representation has the most stable result: firms with more female directors have a significantly lower probability of restatement. Additional tests indicate that ownership type moderates the association with CEO duality but not the associations with board independence or female representation. These results show that board attributes differ in their relation to reporting outcomes and that the consequences of leadership structure depend on institutional context.

title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures
summary: Abstract We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.

title: Accountability Beyond ESG Disclosure: Credibility, Governance Integrity, and the Sustainability‐Signaling Gap in European Finance
summary: ABSTRACT This study addresses significant limitations in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) evaluation by transcending disclosure‐based metrics and presenting a credibility‐focused analytical methodology that assesses the congruence between sustainability signals and substantive performance. Departing from interpretations of ESG that focus solely on disclosure, this study conceptualizes ESG governance as an accountability‐driven process. It introduces the sustainability‐signaling gap as a quantifiable measure of ESG credibility. Drawing upon signaling and legitimacy theory, a combined fuzzy multi‐criteria decision‐making (MCDM) framework is constructed. This framework incorporates the fuzzy best–worst method, the measurement of alternatives and ranking according to compromise solution ranking model, and a diagnostic sustainability gap index (SGI). The framework is then applied to a representative sample of 377 publicly traded European financial institutions spanning the years 2021 to 2024. This analysis utilizes governance quality, disclosure integrity, ESG performance, and environmental outcome indicators obtained from Refinitiv. The greatest calibrated importance is assigned to green‐asset alignment and governance quality in the findings, while disclosure integrity remains central to diagnosing the correspondence between measured performance and sustainability communication. A recurring disparity between ESG signaling and tangible sustainability results is evident throughout the industry, indicating that disclosure‐based strategies often coincide with limited substantive governance and environmental performance. By pinpointing systematic tendencies of both excessive and insufficient signaling, the SGI offers a performance‐focused diagnostic instrument for assessing ESG accountability. This study advances the fields of corporate social responsibility and sustainability governance by translating legitimacy and signaling theory into an actionable assessment framework, thereby providing regulators, supervisors, and financial institutions with a replicable method for identifying superficial ESG practices and enhancing accountability within sustainable finance.

title: INVESTOR BEHAVIOUR IN THE DIGITAL FINANCIAL ECOSYSTEM: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW
summary: Structured Abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study is to undertake the systematic review of academic paper on digital and financial technology to describe the impact of various digital and financial technologies on the behaviour of retail investor under several cognitive and influence their investment decision-making. The study includes internet, social media and social trading platform as a advanced communication channel and social trading application and a financial technology facilitating in execution of trading decision. Study design/methodology/approach: A systematic literature review has been conducted of 94 academic work which includes published journals, conference proceedings, working papers and published books with the systematic search of academic works from several electronic databases to identify relevant studies even though there was research work released between 2000 and 2023. The publication of notable works began in 2014. The search terms included "technological advancements," "internet," "social media," "social trading applications," "trading applications”, "retail investors," "investor behaviour," and "investment decision-making and fintech. Findings: The paper suggest that the digital and financial technological variable collectively impact investor in not only in providing with financial information but also in decision making and trade execution. The increased accessibility to information and trading avenues has led to challenges, such as information overload and the potential for overconfidence in decision-making which results in impulsive and frequent trading affecting their return. Moreover, digital communication technology such as social media, one of the essential sources of information and opinion, also is to be credited with impacting investor sentiment and behaviour leading to herd behaviour and suboptimal return. Research limitations/implications: This paper reports that investors’ behaviour post digital and financial technology adoption have high potential for further study by various stakeholders in the field of behavioural finance from academia, practitioners to regulators. Practical implications: The paper summarizes the lessons which is of importance for the retail investor, implies that retail investor should be careful in relying too much on the digital technology in terms of fetching financial information and trade execution especially when they are not financial experts. Social implications: Under this study, investors can recognize various cognitive biases that can influence their trading behavior and impact their returns. title: Stakeholder Collaboration and Environmental Sustainability in Development Initiatives across South-South Nigeria: A Critical Discourse Analysis
summary: Stakeholder participation has become a vital factor in achieving environmental sustainability in development projects, especially in ecologically sensitive areas such as South-South Nigeria. This study looked into how engaging stakeholders can impact sustainable environmental results in development initiatives marked by oil exploration, biodiversity loss, and ongoing socio-environmental conflicts. The study employed participatory development theory and stakeholder theory; the research used a mixed-methods approach, gathering survey data from community members, government agencies, and corporate representatives, along with qualitative insights from key informant interviews. The findings revealed that when stakeholders are included, it boosts environmental accountability, fosters local ownership, and allows for the incorporation of indigenous knowledge into project design and execution. On the flip side, when engagement is limited or merely symbolic, it often leads to environmental harm, community backlash, and project failures. The study also highlighted that issues such as power imbalances, weak institutional frameworks, and poor communication channels can hinder effective participation. Interestingly, corporate social responsibility efforts by multinational oil companies showed varying levels of success, largely depending on how deeply they involve the community and the transparency of their processes. The research emphasised the importance of participatory governance structures that focus on equity, dialogue, and ongoing engagement among all stakeholders. Ultimately, it concludes that achieving environmental sustainability in the South-South region hinges on meaningful stakeholder involvement throughout all phases of development planning and implementation. The policy recommendations stress the need to strengthen regulatory institutions, build community capacity, and encourage multi-stakeholder partnerships to promote environmentally responsible and socially inclusive development outcomes in the area.

title: Impacts of Financial and Sustainability Measures on Shareholder Value Added based on Resource-based View and Modern Organisational Performance Theories: An Econometric Analysis
summary: This empirical study investigates the most important financial and sustainability performance measures that contribute to shareholder value added (SVA). We employ econometric modelling, with a particular emphasis on simultaneous equation system analysis. We carefully selected resources from the resource-based view (RBV) to identify the capabilities to define the main variables for S&P 500 companies. To obtain consistent and efficient estimates, we employ a seemingly unrelated regression (SURE) method. For each equation in the system, we use a causality framework that includes tests for stationarity, cointegration, and causality. Additionally, we estimate an error-correction model and a cointegration regression to identify long-run relationships. Our sample covers 503 companies in the Standard & Poor’s index over 20 years (2005-2024). We used Stata 19.5 and EViews 12 to conduct the econometric analysis.First, our analysis provides evidence that the three main resources of the resource-based view theory are key to shareholder value added, and that the chosen variables (capabilities) are significant. Second, the variables are cointegrated, and we successfully estimated cointegration regressions for each equation in the system. Third, the error-correction terms are significant in the error-correction models, confirming their role in the process of adjusting to deviations from the long-run equilibrium.Our empirical study focuses on financial and sustainability performance measures. The analysis is performed at the company level and encompasses all sectors of the economy, as in the S&P 500. This approach differs from previous studies that compared industrial and financial companies separately and generally focused on only certain sustainability measures. We analyse the environmental, social, and governance (ESG) scores separately.

title: From FinTech Adoption to Financial Resilience: How FinTech Assimilation, Digital Cash-Flow Visibility, and Cybersecurity Readiness Shape MSME Capability Development
summary: The increasing adoption of financial technology (FinTech) among micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) has created new opportunities for improving financial resilience; however, the mechanisms through which digital technologies generate resilience capabilities remain insufficiently understood, particularly in rural emerging economies. This study examines how FinTech assimilation influences MSME financial resilience by investigating the mediating role of digital cash-flow visibility and the moderating role of cybersecurity readiness. Using a quantitative explanatory approach, data were collected from 228 MSMEs in Soppeng Regency, Indonesia, and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that FinTech assimilation significantly enhances MSME financial resilience, with digital cash-flow visibility serving as a key mediating mechanism that transforms digital financial resources into actionable financial capabilities. Furthermore, cybersecurity readiness significantly conditions the relationship between FinTech assimilation and digital cash-flow visibility, highlighting the importance of complementary security capabilities in digital transformation. This study contributes to the FinTech and MSME resilience literature by shifting the focus from technology adoption toward post-adoption capability development. The findings provide practical implications for MSMEs, policymakers, and FinTech providers in designing sustainable digital transformation strategies.

title: How Technological Capability Accumulation Reshapes Industrial Competitiveness
summary: This paper examines the relationship between innovation, research and development (R&D), technological transformation, and industrial competitiveness in an environment characterized by rapid technological and organizational change. The literature reviewed shows that competitiveness increasingly depends on firms’ capacity to accumulate technological knowledge, absorb external information, protect and commercialize intellectual property, and transform research expenditure into sustained productivity improvements. The paper also considers the effects of Industry 4.0, artificial intelligence, robotics, digital platforms, FinTech, and blockchain on industrial performance, emphasizing that technological adoption generates stronger results when supported by adequate organizational capabilities, skills, data resources, and managerial practices. A further dimension concerns the increasing integration of environmental sustainability with industrial strategy through green innovation, digital supply chains, servitization, and resilience-oriented production systems. The literature indicates that these transformations are influenced by institutional conditions, industrial policies, competitive pressures, and innovation ecosystems. Overall, the paper argues that contemporary industrial competitiveness cannot be explained by technological investment alone. It results from interactions among R&D, organizational capabilities, external knowledge, human capital, digital transformation, sustainability strategies, institutional quality, and the capacity of firms to commercialize and operationalize technological advances.

title: SOFTWARE SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY: A TAXONOMY OF ATTACKS AND A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF PROVENANCE-BASED COUNTERMEASURES
summary: This article analyses the security of the software supply chain, which has become one of the fastest-growing attack surfaces in modern information systems. A five-stage reference model of the supply chain with explicit trust boundaries is proposed, and a taxonomy of attacks is derived from it in which every class is bound to a concrete injection point: source tampering, dependency abuse, build injection, artifact substitution and delivery tampering. The verification problem is stated formally as a predicate over signed build provenance, and the resulting conditions are then used as evaluation criteria. On this basis the principal countermeasures — the software bill of materials (SPDX and CycloneDX), signed build provenance (in-toto and the SLSA Build levels), artifact signing and reproducible builds — are compared with respect to the attack classes they actually mitigate rather than the guarantees they are commonly assumed to provide. The analysis is validated against the XZ Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094). It is shown that a bill of materials and a valid artifact signature would not have prevented that attack, whereas a hermetic build at SLSA Build Level 3 combined with reproducible builds breaks its central mechanism — the divergence between the released source archive and the publicly auditable repository. The residual gap between declared and auditable build inputs is formalised and proposed as a practical assurance metric. The compliance of the examined mechanisms with the legislation of the Republic of Uzbekistan and with international regulation is substantiated. The results indicate that supply chain assurance should be designed as a verification chain over the build process rather than as an inventory of components.

title: Optimizing Seafood Production Systems: An Integrated IoT Architecture and Cost-Benefit Analysis for Real-Time Operational Transparency
summary: The seafood processing industry faces critical operational challenges in maintaining mass-balance integrity because manual, paper-based recording causes data lag and human input errors. This study aims to optimize PT XYZ's seafood production system by developing an integrated Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) architecture and evaluating its economic feasibility for real-time operational transparency. Employing a participatory mixed-method approach, the methodology integrates qualitative data analysis (in-depth interviews, Empathy Mapping, and Point-of-View synthesis via Design Thinking) alongside quantitative data analysis (Digital Maturity Assessment scoring on a 1–5 scale, Usability Testing metrics, and Cost-Benefit Analysis modeling). Lean Startup iterations further validated the Minimum Viable Architecture (MVA). The results show that the proposed system optimizes shop-floor production by enabling real-time data acquisition via water-resistant sensors, edge gateways, and RESTful API integration with the local ERP, effectively eliminating operational data lag. Quantitatively, the Cost-Benefit Analysis confirms the project’s economic viability, revealing an initial investment of IDR 665,675,000 against annual operational savings of IDR 240,000,000, yielding a 36.05% Return on Investment (ROI) and a payback period of 2.77 years. Ultimately, this framework optimizes production systems by improving mass-balance accuracy, operational transparency, and managerial decision-making, providing a scalable digital transformation roadmap for the seafood manufacturing sector.

title: Cenários prospectivos e análise de riscos no planejamento estratégico de pequenas e médias empresas em ambientes competitivos
summary: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) increasingly operate in environments marked by economic volatility, regulatory change and technological disruption that undermine strategic planning models based on linear projections. This article aims to analyze the contribution of the prospective scenario method, combined with systematic risk analysis, to qualifying the strategic planning of SMEs operating in competitive environments. This is a descriptive, qualitative bibliographic review grounded in the French school of strategic foresight (Godet), the Anglo-Saxon scenario planning tradition (Wack; Schwartz; Van der Heijden), risk management frameworks (ISO 31000) and institutional publications on SME governance and sustainability (OECD; IBGC; SEBRAE). The analysis indicates that scenario building, by exploring multiple future hypotheses rather than single projections, broadens SME managers' capacity for anticipation, reduces founder-centered decision bias and creates conditions for integrating strategic planning, risk management and corporate governance. The article also discusses the need to adapt classical foresight tools — originally developed for large corporations and governments — to the reality of limited resources, lean structures and informal decision-making typical of SMEs. It is concluded that incorporating, even in a simplified and proportional way, scenario-building and risk-analysis practices into the strategic planning process is a relevant vector of resilience, competitiveness and sustainability for SMEs, particularly when articulated with minimal governance structures.

title: ULE Framework — Codebook and Scoring Protocol
summary: The method for applying the Urban Living Lab Legal Enablement (ULE) framework: condition definitions, scoring scale, scope restriction, decision rules and coding procedure. It contains no empirical scoring data. Scoring records for individual case sets are deposited as separate records and cite this one as their methodological source. The separation is deliberate: the protocol is reusable independently of any particular case, and can be applied by other researchers to jurisdictions not covered here. WHY THE FRAMEWORK EXISTS Living lab scholarship documents extensively that ecology-oriented labs fail to become institutionally durable. It does not provide a way to identify which institutional condition is missing in a given case. Aggregate judgements do not support targeted intervention; condition-level diagnosis does. THE FIVE CONDITIONS E1 Statutory Enactment · E2 Governance Empowerment · E3 Financial Endowment · E4 Evidentiary Mandate · E5 Epistemic Translation. The conditions are sequential: each is a precondition for the functional operation of those that follow. FOUR RULES A READER SHOULD KNOW BEFORE READING A SCORING RECORD Scope restriction. Conditions are assessed against provision specifically enabling ecology-oriented urban living labs, not against general environmental regulatory capacity. A low score is not a judgement about the quality of environmental governance. Level and form are recorded separately. The score records degree of enablement; provision_form records the type of provision relied upon. Two jurisdictions may score equally while relying on structurally different provisions. Cross-case learning potential derives from difference in form, not in level. Legal force, tier and durability are three different questions, recorded in three separate fields. Whether a provision binds (rule 6.8), what it does to the activity (rule 6.9), and how withdrawable the obligation is (rule 6.10) do not answer each other. A provision can be binding and still only facilitate; two provisions of equal score can differ sharply in how easily they are withdrawn. Contested scores are a procedural declaration, not a confidence rating (rule 6.6). The mark records that the evidence admitted two adjacent values and that a staged double reading was therefore performed. A cell not marked contested is not thereby more certain in a general sense. TWO VERSION NUMBERS, AND WHY THEY DIFFER Two numbering systems run alongside each other and are stated here because earlier descriptions conflated them. The codebook document carries its own version number, which is now 3.1. Zenodo increments a separate record version on each upload, and this upload is record version 6. Earlier record versions carried codebook documents v1.0 and v2.0; the description of record version 5 referred to that upload as "VERSION 5.0", which named the record rather than the document it contained. Codebook v3.0 was prepared but never deposited, and its content reaches a published record here for the first time. A citation should name the codebook version; a link should use the DOI. WHAT CODEBOOK VERSION 3.1 ADDS A maintenance revision arising from application of the protocol to a fifth case set. No condition definition, no point on the scale and no partial/substantial boundary changes, and no score in any deposited record is affected. Rule 6.6 now defines the three fields that record the staged double reading: candidate_scores, contested_reason and reread_status. The procedure itself is unchanged. It was previously recorded in a single flag, which did not let a reader see which of the two adjacent values were in question, on what ground the provision was ambiguous, or whether the second reading had actually been performed. A flag can be set without the reading having happened; three fields cannot be filled without it. Rule 6.8 gains a fourth value, mixed, for a cell whose provisions differ in legal force. The scoring rule is unchanged: the score still follows the weakest class that is doing necessary work. The addition governs how the source is described, not how the cell is scored, so that a reader is not told a cell rests on a binding instrument when the limb carrying it to its ceiling is guidance. Where mixed is recorded, each limb and its class must be named in the coding reasoning. Section 9 records all four additions in the required-fields table. WHAT REACHES A PUBLISHED RECORD FOR THE FIRST TIME HERE Rule 6.8, legal force in three classes, with the rule that a score follows the weakest class doing necessary work. Rule 6.9, three tiers of legal condition — authorises, facilitates, does not prohibit — recorded in legal_condition_tier. Rule 6.10, durability of the provision relied upon, classes L1 to L4, read from where the obligation arises rather than from the size of the programme. Section 2.2, indicators and data types per condition. Section 4.1, what a score does not depend on. Section 8, the procedure for applying the protocol consistently across jurisdictions. The coding procedure runs to nine steps. COMPATIBILITY Records scored under v1.0, v2.0 or v3.0 remain valid and are not invalidated. A record that does not carry the three new fields is incomplete under v3.1 rather than wrong under the version it was scored under. Every version remains citable at its own version DOI, and the full version history is in section 13 of the codebook. FILES IN THIS VERSION ULE_codebook_v3.1.md — the full codebook: five conditions, scale, scope restriction, decision rules 6.1 to 6.10, nine-step coding procedure, cross-jurisdiction consistency procedure, required-field specification.ULE_Codebook_v3.1.pdf — the same document as a formatted PDF.scoring_template.csv — empty scoring record with the required fields.document_inventory_template.csv — empty corpus inventory with the required fields. TWO VERSION NUMBERS, AND WHY THEY DIFFER Two numbering systems run alongside each other and are stated here because earlier descriptions conflated them. The codebook document carries its own version number, which is now 3.1. Zenodo increments a separate record version on each upload, and this upload is record version 6. Earlier record versions carried codebook documents v1.0 and v2.0; the description of record version 5 referred to that upload as "VERSION 5.0", which named the record rather than the document it contained. Codebook v3.0 was prepared but never deposited, and its content reaches a published record here for the first time. A citation should name the codebook version; a link should use the DOI. WHAT CODEBOOK VERSION 3.1 ADDS A maintenance revision arising from application of the protocol to a fifth case set. No condition definition, no point on the scale and no partial/substantial boundary changes, and no score in any deposited record is affected. Rule 6.6 now defines the three fields that record the staged double reading: candidate_scores, contested_reason and reread_status. The procedure itself is unchanged. It was previously recorded in a single flag, which did not let a reader see which of the two adjacent values were in question, on what ground the provision was ambiguous, or whether the second reading had actually been performed. A flag can be set without the reading having happened; three fields cannot be filled without it. Rule 6.8 gains a fourth value, mixed, for a cell whose provisions differ in legal force. The scoring rule is unchanged: the score still follows the weakest class that is doing necessary work. The addition governs how the source is described, not how the cell is scored, so that a reader is not told a cell rests on a binding instrument when the limb carrying it to its ceiling is guidance. Where mixed is recorded, each limb and its class must be named in the coding reasoning. Section 9 records all four additions in the required-fields table. WHAT REACHES A PUBLISHED RECORD FOR THE FIRST TIME HERE Rule 6.8, legal force in three classes, with the rule that a score follows the weakest class doing necessary work. Rule 6.9, three tiers of legal condition — authorises, facilitates, does not prohibit — recorded in legal_condition_tier. Rule 6.10, durability of the provision relied upon, classes L1 to L4, read from where the obligation arises rather than from the size of the programme. Section 2.2, indicators and data types per condition. Section 4.1, what a score does not depend on. Section 8, the procedure for applying the protocol consistently across jurisdictions. The coding procedure runs to nine steps. COMPATIBILITY Records scored under v1.0, v2.0 or v3.0 remain valid and are not invalidated. A record that does not carry the three new fields is incomplete under v3.1 rather than wrong under the version it was scored under. Every version remains citable at its own version DOI, and the full version history is in section 13 of the codebook. title: Development of an Adaptive Curriculum Based on Outcome-Based Education (OBE) in the Information Technology Study Program at UIN Syekh Ali Hasan Ahmad Addary Padangsidimpuan
summary: This study developed an adaptive curriculum based on Outcome-Based Education (OBE) for the Information Technology Study Program at UIN Syekh Ali Hasan Ahmad Addary Padangsidimpuan. The curriculum redesign aimed to directly align Course Learning Outcomes (CPMK) with Graduate Learning Outcomes (CPL), structured progressively across semesters to support competency formation through conceptual understanding, laboratory practice, and project-based assignments. Internal document analysis and academic discussions revealed gaps in vertical and horizontal alignment among learning outcomes, particularly in core areas such as programming, systems analysis, and digital business. The revised curriculum integrates project-based learning into at least 60% of core courses and embeds Islamic ethical values and local contexts into the learning design. Validation conducted by internal faculty teams confirmed that the curriculum is feasible and that the course mapping is relevant. The results indicate that a transparent and reflective internal process supported by institutional documentation can produce a curriculum that is responsive to the digital transformation era, even without involving external experts or alumni surveys. These findings provide practical implications for curriculum policy in Islamic higher education institutions and open opportunities for further research to assess the long-term impact of OBE implementation on graduate outcomes

title: How can manufacturing firms transform green collaboration into sustainable innovation? Unpacking the sustainable supply chain finance and stakeholder pathways in Ghana
summary: Purpose Grounded in the natural resource-based view and contingency theory, this study investigates how green supply chain collaboration enhances sustainable business model innovation. It explores the mediating role of sustainable supply chain finance and the moderating effects of stakeholder pressures in shaping these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Data collected from 300 managers of manufacturing firms in Ghana were analysed using structural equation modelling to empirically test the proposed hypotheses. Findings Green supply chain collaboration significantly influences sustainable business model innovation, with sustainable supply chain finance serving as a crucial mediating mechanism. Organisational stakeholder pressures moderate the relationship between green collaboration and sustainable finance, while regulatory pressures show no significant moderating effect. Research limitations/implications This study advances understanding of how collaborative green practices translate into business model innovation through financial mechanisms, suggesting further research is needed on contextual factors affecting these relationships. Practical implications The findings guide manufacturing managers in leveraging supply chain collaboration to achieve sustainable innovation. They demonstrate that sustainable finance amplifies collaborative benefits, while organisational stakeholder engagement strengthens implementation effectiveness. Originality/value The findings enrich academic discourse by establishing sustainable supply chain finance as a critical pathway linking collaboration to innovation. This research highlights how financial and collaborative mechanisms jointly enable sustainable transformation in emerging economy manufacturing contexts.

title: PENERAPAN FUNGSI DASAR MANAJEMEN PENDIDIKAN ISLAM DALAM MANAJEMEN BERBASIS TEKNOLOGI DI PESANTREN MODERN
summary: The digital transformation occurring within Islamic educational institutions requires a more adaptive and professional management system capable of meeting the demands for efficiency, accountability, and quality improvement. This study aims to analyze the implementation of fundamental Islamic educational management functions (POAC: Planning, Organizing, Actuating, Controlling) within a technology-based management system at Al-Ma'soem Islamic Boarding School, as well as to identify the challenges and opportunities emerging from this digitalization process. Employing a qualitative field-study design, data were collected through in-depth interviews, limited observations, and document analysis related to the digital management system. The findings indicate that planning, organizing, actuating, and controlling have been integrated through the use of management information systems, digital-competence-based staff recruitment, the utilization of digital administrative and learning applications, and monitoring mechanisms supported by dashboards and content-filtering systems. The results confirm that digitalization enhances the effectiveness of pesantren governance, although its success depends heavily on human resource readiness, infrastructure stability, and an organizational culture supportive of innovation. Theoretically, this study expands the discourse on Islamic educational management by offering the POAC-Digital concept, which integrates technological adaptation with Islamic values. Practically, the findings provide a strategic reference for developing modern pesantren management models that are more effective, accountable, and quality-oriented.

title: Protecting Workers' Right to Mental Health in Digital Work Environments: Legal Challenges and Reform Directions in Vietnam
summary: Digital work technologies increasingly determine when, how, and at what intensity work is performed. Continuous connectivity, electronic monitoring, algorithmic management, and technology-enabled harassment can generate psychosocial risks that are not adequately addressed by legal rules designed mainly for physical workplaces. This article asks whether Vietnamese labour and occupational safety and health law provides a coherent preventive framework for protecting workers’ mental health in digital work environments and which comparative models can guide reform. It uses doctrinal analysis, interdisciplinary literature synthesis, and functional comparison with international standards and selected approaches in the European Union, France, and Australia. The analysis finds that Vietnamese law contains relevant constitutional, working-time, occupational safety and health, dignity, anti-harassment, and personal-data safeguards, but these rules remain fragmented. In particular, psychosocial risks are not expressly defined or systematically assessed; workers have no statutory right to disconnect; electronic monitoring and algorithmic management are not regulated as working-condition issues; and protection for platform and remote workers remains incomplete. The article proposes an integrated reform model built around seven elements: express recognition of mental health and psychosocial risks; mandatory risk assessment and control; a qualified right to disconnect; transparency, consultation, and human review for digital monitoring and algorithmic decisions; confidential support and return-to-work measures; stronger social dialogue, inspection, and national data; and appropriately extended protection for platform workers. The proposed model treats mental health protection as a preventive labour-law obligation and a condition of sustainable digital transformation rather than as a discretionary employee benefit.

title: Will the Capital Markets Union Revive European Growth?
summary: Abstract The EU Capital Markets Union initiative is supposed to further integrate and strengthen European capital markets. However, the Commission’s current agenda fails to harmonize the national markets on one competitive framework. Instead, the Taxonomy Regulation adds a new layer of rules on top of the existing barriers. The proposal of a common safe asset – a frequent demand in the context of the Capital Markets Union – would weaken member states’ willingness to address structural problems through comprehensive market reforms. Consequently, the current agenda further harms the attractiveness of European capital markets instead of improving them. A genuine Capital Markets Union would require the EU to abandon its path of top-down harmonization and allow competition among national frameworks to determine the best rules.

title: Integrating benefits realization management into Industry 4.0 project implementation: a model for manufacturing transformation
summary: Purpose This study proposes an Industry 4.0 project implementation model oriented toward benefits realization management (BRM). It addresses the digitalization paradox, whereby substantial investments in digital technologies fail to translate into tangible organizational value and fills a gap in the literature by integrating BRM and Industry 4.0 into a unified implementation model. Design/methodology/approach The research adopted design science research (DSR), following a seven-step approach. A systematic literature review mapped existing BRM artifacts and identified structural gaps. Semi-structured interviews with 20 industry experts informed the artifact design, while the Delphi method with a panel of 10 experts was employed to iteratively evaluate and refine the model until consensus was reached. Findings The resulting model is structured around three macro-phases (benefits identification, realization and sustainment), nine sequential stages, three operational modes (project, transition and operations) and five decision gates. Crucially, it incorporates cross-cutting pillars, namely leadership, governance and ownership; communication and consensus; risk management and adaptability; focus and organizational culture; and capability and competencies, which permeate the entire life cycle of Industry 4.0 initiatives. Originality/value The model provides an integrative framework combining BRM and Industry 4.0 within a single artifact, extending implementation models that often confine benefits management to early project phases. It offers manufacturing practitioners and researchers a structured and methodologically grounded framework to identify, realize and sustain the expected benefits of digital transformation investments, offering a structured approach to mitigate the risks associated with the digitalization paradox within the industrial sector.

title: Corporate Governance Practices and Financial Performance of Non-Deposit-Taking Saccos in Nairobi City County, Kenya
summary: This study examined the relationship between corporate governance practices (board structure, audit committee effectiveness and internal control systems) and the financial performance of non-deposit-taking Savings and Credit Cooperative Societies (SACCOs) in Nairobi City County, Kenya, and tested whether regulatory compliance moderates these relationships. Evidence on governance and performance in Kenyan SACCOs is concentrated on deposit-taking societies, and national supervisory aggregates cannot show whether governance practices are associated with the profitability and liquidity of non-deposit-taking SACCOs in Nairobi. Evidence on whether regulatory compliance changes these relationships is also limited. Guided by Agency Theory and Stakeholder Theory, the study adopted a quantitative, cross-sectional correlational design with retrospective financial data. From 125 SASRA-authorized non-deposit-taking SACCOs headquartered in Nairobi, 56 were selected by simple random sampling. A structured questionnaire yielded 112 usable responses (two per SACCO; 80.0% response rate), consolidated to SACCO level. Five-year average return on assets (ROA) and liquidity ratio for 2021–2025 were derived from 280 SACCO-year records. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and hierarchical regression with HC3 robust standard errors and Holm-adjusted interaction tests. The study findings show that, when entered together, board structure, audit committee effectiveness and internal control systems demonstrated no statistically significant unique association with ROA (p = .364–.596) or liquidity ratio (p = .669–.980); the models explained 3.9% and 1.8% of the variance, respectively. Regulatory compliance did not significantly moderate any relationship (joint interaction tests: ROA p = .270; liquidity p = .872; all Holm-adjusted p ≥ .476). The governance composites were highly intercorrelated (r = .77–.91). The governance measures examined did not provide statistically significant explanations of differences in ROA or liquidity among the sampled SACCOs. This does not show that governance is unimportant. The study recommends that SACCO boards document and periodically review governance arrangements as accountability practice, that SASRA and the State Department for Cooperatives consider standardized governance disclosures and clear liquidity-ratio reporting conventions, and that future research use objective governance indicators and longitudinal designs. title: Beyond Digital Adoption: ICT and Healthcare Service Delivery in Catholic Faith-Based Level II Dispensaries in Kajiado North and Kajiado East Sub-Counties, Kenya
summary: Digital transformation is increasingly becoming an important component of primary healthcare service delivery. However, the contribution of information and communication technology (ICT) in small faith-based primary healthcare facilities depends not only on the availability of digital technologies but also on the organizational and infrastructural conditions within which they are used. This study explored how ICT integration influences healthcare service delivery in Catholic faith-based Level II dispensaries in Kajiado North and Kajiado East Sub-Counties, Kenya. A qualitative multiple-case study design was employed across five Catholic faith-based Level II dispensaries. Data were generated from 48 unique participants comprising five administrators and departmental heads, 23 clinical and support staff, 15 patients, and five community representatives. Semi-structured interviews were complemented by two focus group discussions drawn from the same participant pool. Thematic analysis generated three themes: ICT-enabled communication, ICT influence on access, and ICT communication and digital-service challenges. ICT-enabled communication was identified across 28 of the 48 participant cases (58.3%); ICT communication and digital-service challenges across 25 cases (52.1%); and ICT influence on access across 23 cases (47.9%). Participants associated ICT with record keeping, information retrieval, communication, reporting, coordination, patient follow-up, and service reminders. Unreliable internet connectivity, power interruptions, limited equipment, inadequate training, and technical-support needs constrained consistent digital use. The study concludes that ICT supports healthcare service delivery through communication, information management, coordination, and selected access mechanisms, but its contribution depends on infrastructure, staff capacity, technical support, and organizational conditions.

title: BRSR 2.0 and Mandatory ESG Assurance: Is India Moving towards Audit-based Sustainability Governance?
summary: In the span of just over a decade, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”) has moved India's listed firms from voluntary sustainability reporting towards a progressively mandatory, independently verified ESG ("Environmental, Social and Governance") disclosure regime. The launch in July 2023 of a new category of Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (the “BRSR Core”), together with the ease-of-doing-business relaxations of March 2025, has introduced a hybrid ‘assessment or assurance’ paradigm that borrows both the vocabulary and, more significantly, the legal gravitas of statutory financial auditing. The scope of this paper is limited only to the Standard Core Disclosures for BRSR as required by SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and does not include the voluntary ESG Ratings, ESG labelled investment products and environmental clearances granted for sectors under a dedicated approach. This paper analyses whether this shift amounts to a transformation toward audit-based sustainability governance in India. It argues that although SEBI has made ESG reporting a compliance requirement under the Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015, there has been no commensurate progress in Indian law regarding the allocation of responsibility for ESG statements and errors among directors, the audit committee, independent directors, assurance providers, and statutory auditors. Based on the analysis of India's corporate jurisprudence, SEBI's enforcement practices, and ESG-related assurance litigation in Australia and the United States, this paper argues that a dedicated statutory blueprint for ESG assurance in India is needed, and that assurance should be a separate regulatory function, with specific liability rules, to close the enforcement gap that currently leaves unverified sustainability claims unpunished.

title: Determinants and Configurational Pathways of Quantification in Corporate Environmental Disclosure: Evidence from Kazakhstan
summary: This study examines firm-level characteristics associated with quantitative disclosure breadth (QDB) and the configurations associated with high QDB in Kazakhstan. It combines ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). The analysis is organized around three theoretical elements: external information demand, information production capacity, and disclosure oversight and incentives. These elements are represented by five firm-level conditions: environmentally sensitive industry (ESI), firm size (Size), profitability (ROA), board independence (Indep), and state ownership (SOE). It uses a sample of 56 KASE-listed firms, comprising 145 firm-year observations from 2021 to 2024. The OLS results show that Indep and ESI are show significant positive associations with QDB, while Size, ROA, and SOE do not show significant average net associations. The association between Indep and QDB becomes statistically insignificant in the continuous-sample robustness test. The fsQCA results identify four equifinal configurations associated with high QDB, with an overall solution coverage of 0.3664. S1–S3 remain stable across the robustness tests, whereas S4 is sensitive to specification choices. The study contributes by distinguishing QDB as a distinct quantitative disclosure dimension and by showing how firm-level characteristics are associated with QDB through both net associations and configurational patterns.

title: Blockchain for Supply Chain Transparency in Fast Fashion: A Scoping Review of Primary Studies, Implementation Barriers, and Sustainability Pathways
summary: Fast-fashion supply chains are under pressure to deliver greater traceability, provenance, accountability, and measurable sustainability outcomes, yet the evidence base for blockchain-enabled transparency remains uneven.This scoping review mapped primary research on blockchain applications for supply-chain transparency in fast fashion and directly transferable textile-apparel contexts.In this review, fast fashion is defined by compressed product cycles, high stock-keeping-unit turnover, frequent sourcing changes, intense buyer-driven price pressure, and extensive subcontracting.The search concept from the retained review record was translated into six standard bibliographic databases, and the numerically verified screening set comprised 122 de-duplicated records.After title/abstract screening and full-text assessment, 31 primary studies published between 2020 and 2025 were included.Data were charted on study design, setting, blockchain architecture, transparency function, implementation stage, reported outcome, barrier, enabler, and sustainability implication.The synthesis distinguishes findings specific to fast-fashion or apparel supply chains from transferable evidence derived from adjacent textile-fiber settings.Blockchain most consistently enabled tamper-resistant provenance records, auditready documentation, product authentication, and more granular environmental accounting when combined with the Internet of Things (IoT), radio frequency identification (RFID), and quick response (QR) identifiers, enterprise systems, or digital product passports.However, direct evidence of social-sustainability effects, such as improved labor rights, wages, working conditions, or grievance resolution, remained limited.The review therefore supports a qualified conclusion: blockchain is a conditional transparency infrastructure rather than an isolated technological solution, and its value depends on credible source-data capture, supplier incentives, governance arrangements, and policy standards that connect material traceability with environmental, economic, and social accountability.

title: THE IMPACT OF TRANSFORMATIONAL LEADERSHIP AND GOOD CORPORATE GOVERNANCE ON JOB PERFORMANCE: A META-ANALYSIS
summary: Performance plays a significant role in achieving organizational goals, fostering competitiveness, and maintaining sustainability. Earlier investigations demonstrate that transformative leadership and sound corporate governance (GCG) considerably influence performance. Nevertheless, an exhaustive integration of empirical results is essential to clarify the intensity and coherence of this connection. This report use quantitative meta-analysis to assess the influence of transformative leadership and governance on performance outcomes. We rigorously identified 32 empirical research articles published between 2021 and 2026 from the Google Scholar, Scopus, and ScienceDirect databases. Utilizing JASP, we determined impact sizes and analyzed heterogeneity via a random-effects model. The assessment demonstrated that transformational leadership (r = 0.378) and GCG (r = 0.172) significantly positively impacted employee performance (p < 0.01). Transformational leadership exhibited a greater influence. The investigation identified diversity across the research and lacked evidence of publication bias. These conclusions are consistent with the prevailing research, underscoring the crucial impact of transformational leadership and GCG in elevating performance. The outcomes emphasize the importance of transformational leadership and effective corporate governance in boosting company performance. As a result, pragmatic advice involves establishing focused transformational leadership training and corporate policies that foster GCG to boost performance.

title: Typology of Digital Transformations in Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises
summary: The article is devoted to the study of the problems of digital transformation of organizations. The key concepts and classifications are analyzed, highlighting D. Winter's approaches, the interpretative approach, the process approach, the OMI classification, the basic technology approach, technological intensity, and others. The typologization of digital changes in an organization makes it possible to understand the depth of the phenomenon of transformation itself, to identify the strengths and weaknesses of deterministic approaches. As the number of digital transformations in organizations increases and the associated cost of implementing digital technologies increases, the importance of a deep understanding of the nature of transformational changes increases. As part of the work, the author proposed a new typology of digital transformation that combines various classification features and is applicable in the context of dynamic transformations in the organization, which is typical for developing systems. A practical tool for implementing the proposed classification is the digital transformation matrix, which reveals the essence of frontal, structural and process changes in the implementation of digital initiatives. The combination of the control object with the type of technology used can form various types of dynamic changes. The research results have the potential to be used for practical business analysis purposes in the planning and implementation of complex digital change projects in organizations. Also, the main conclusions of the work can be applied for further scientific research of the phenomenon of digital transformation in all its diversity.

title: MECHANISMS FOR IMPROVING MANAGEMENT EFFICIENCY THROUGH DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
summary: Using commercial banks as the case, the paper substantiates mechanisms for raising management efficiency through digital transformation. In 2021-2024 mobile transaction value per service outlet rose from UZS 4.9 billion to UZS 28.1 billion (5.8 times), yet the number of outlets grew by 18.7% and the cost-to-income ratio worsened from 33% to 36%. Parallel expansion of digital and physical channels limits management efficiency. Mechanisms of strategic management, data-driven decisions, process automation, organizational redesign and risk management, together with a KPI system, are proposed.

summary: The paper assesses the effect of green finance on the financial stability and competitiveness of commercial banks in Uzbekistan. Green finance affects banks through funding diversification and risk management, but its scale remains limited.

title: The paradox of government-guided green funds: an exacerbating effect on corporate ESG greenwashing
summary: The government-guided green funds (GGFs) are pivotal policy-oriented financial instruments designed to channel capital toward green development sectors, but their impact on corporate ESG governance remains less explored and warrants in-depth investigation. Using panel data from China’s A-share listed companies between 2012 and 2022, this study employs a multi-period difference-in-differences approach to investigate the effect and mechanisms of GGFs on corporate ESG greenwashing. The results indicate that GGFs have an exacerbating effect on corporate ESG greenwashing, a conclusion that remains valid after a series of robustness tests. Mechanism analysis indicates that GGFs exacerbate corporate ESG greenwashing via increasing common institutional ownership and heightening environmental regulatory pressure. Additionally, heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect of GGFs is stronger in private enterprises, non-heavily-polluting industries, firms with low information transparency and those with high managerial myopia. Spillover analysis reveals that GGFs generate negative intra-industry yet positive intra-regional spillover effects on corporate ESG greenwashing. This study provides critical theoretical foundations and policy implications for governments to optimize the operational mechanisms, capital allocation, and post-investment management of GGFs.

title: Smart Multi-Species Milk Bank System (SM²BS) Integrating Cold Chain Management, Digital Traceability, and Nutritional Profiling of Cow, Goat, Sheep, Mare, and Buffalo Milk
summary: The Smart Multi-Species Milk Bank System (SM²BS) is proposed as an integrated digital platform to improve milk supply chain management through cold chain management, digital traceability, and nutritional profiling. This study adopts a qualitative approach involving literature review, observation of milk handling processes, and stakeholder discussions to identify operational challenges and develop a conceptual framework for managing cow, goat, sheep, mare, and buffalo milk. Building on the existing Smart Milk Bank System (SMBS) prototype and preliminary goat milk quality testing conducted with CV Cahaya Firdaus, the proposed system integrates batch identification, quality records, storage conditions, and comparative nutritional data. Its disruptive novelty lies in connecting multi-species nutritional intelligence with cold chain monitoring and end-to-end traceability within a unified digital ecosystem. The framework is expected to support improved transparency, quality management, inventory coordination, and informed decision-making across milk supply chains. However, the proposed multi-species functionality and its operational benefits require further implementation and validation. This study provides a conceptual foundation for developing a more integrated, data-driven milk bank system and strengthening dairy supply chain resilience.

title: Pathways to sustainable business model transformation: corporate governance, strategic leadership and business strategy
summary: Purpose In today’s rapidly evolving business environment, firms face increasing pressure to adopt sustainable practices, with the circular economy (CE) model emerging as a transformative pathway toward environmental and economic resilience. This study aims to investigate the role of governance mechanisms, particularly board and chief executive officer (CEO) dynamics, in enhancing CE performance among manufacturing firms in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. In addition, it examines the moderating role of business strategy in the relationship between governance mechanisms and CE performance, with a focus on innovation, resource efficiency and operational sustainability. Design/methodology/approach The analysis uses panel data from 6,929 firm-year observations and applies dynamic panel estimation techniques, including the system generalized method of moments, to assess the effects of governance, leadership and strategy on CE performance. To strengthen causal inference and ensure robustness, this study incorporates lagged variables, two-stage least squares, propensity score matching and generalized least squares. Findings The results show that board interlock, independence, expertise, CEO foreign experience and external roles significantly enhance CE performance, while concentrated ownership and long CEO tenure constrain it. Business strategy acts as both a direct driver of CE adoption and a moderator that amplifies governance and leadership effects. Heterogeneity across industries reveals that governance plays a stronger role in resource-intensive sectors such as energy and chemicals, while consumer-driven sectors such as food and beverages are shaped more by market pressures and regulatory demands. Originality/value This study extends agency theory by showing that governance mechanisms can act as both enablers and barriers to CE adoption and refines the resource-based view by demonstrating that leadership attributes are valuable resources only when contextually relevant and practically applied. By situating these dynamics within the institutional realities of the MENA region, this study reveals how governance and leadership can substitute for weak institutions, while business strategy serves as a catalyst that translates governance potential into sustainability outcomes. The findings advance theoretical understanding of the governance–sustainability nexus and provide actionable insights for managers, policymakers and stakeholders aiming to accelerate CE adoption and support sustainability transitions in emerging markets.

title: The Effect of Relational Resources on Supply Chain Robustness: The Moderating Role of Relational Capital
summary: Increasing supply chain disruptions have intensified the need for firms to develop capabilities that support operational continuity and effective responses to uncertainty. Although previous studies have examined supply chain robustness through operational and technological perspectives, limited attention has been given to how relational resources influence robustness and how relational capital shapes these relationships. This study examines the effects of resource complementarity and resource specificity on supply chain robustness and investigates the direct and moderating roles of relational capital among firms in the Greater Accra Region of Ghana. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted using structured questionnaires administered to supply chain managers. Of the 384 questionnaires distributed, 296 valid responses were used for analysis. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was performed using SmartPLS. Resource complementarity positively influenced supply chain robustness (β = 0.714, p < 0.001), whereas resource specificity had a significant negative association with robustness (β = −0.305, p = 0.022). Relational capital had a positive direct effect on robustness (β = 0.618, p < 0.001). It also positively moderated the relationship between resource complementarity and robustness (β = 0.292, p < 0.001) and negatively moderated the relationship between resource specificity and robustness (β = −0.197, p = 0.012). The study concludes that relational resources contribute significantly to supply chain robustness, but their effects depend on the nature of the resources and the relational conditions surrounding their use. Firms should strengthen collaboration and combine complementary partner resources while managing relationship-specific investments carefully to avoid unnecessary constraints on operational flexibility.

title: JAPAN’S POLICY ON FORMING INTERNATIONAL HYDROGEN SUPPLY CHAINS IN THE ASIA-PACIFIC REGION
summary: In the context of the global transition to a low-carbon development trajectory, hydrogen is becoming a key element of energy security and decarbonization of the economy. The article is devoted to the analysis of Japan’s policy on the formation of international hydrogen supply chains in the Asia-Pacific region. Japan’s limited domestic energy resources, heavy dependence on imports, and ambitious climate goals make cross-border hydrogen infrastructure a strategic priority for Tokyo. Japan considers the import of low-carbon hydrogen as a tool to ensure sustainable energy supply, diversify energy sources and strengthen technological leadership in promising industries.The paper shows that Japan currently plays a leading role in developing and implementing international hydrogen projects. It is actively building bilateral and multilateral agreements with Asia-Pacific countries, establishing specialized terminals, testing transport and storage technologies, and introducing national standards and certification systems. Increased attention is being paid to institutional mechanisms, public-private partnerships, and financial support that allow Japanese corporations to initiate and coordinate regional initiatives. The study demonstrates that Japan’s policy goes beyond purely energy objectives, forming a sustainable model of technological and economic cooperation capable of shaping the architecture of the future hydrogen trading market in the Asia-Pacific region.The potential remains within the framework of Russian-Japanese cooperation. Russia has significant resources for the production of low-carbon hydrogen, which, combined with Japanese technological and investment opportunities, creates objective conditions for launching joint pilot projects in the Russian Far East. Despite the difficult foreign policy environment, geographical proximity is a factor determining the long-term prospects for cooperation.

title: Supply chain antifragility capabilities: a systematic literature network analysis and conceptual framework
summary: Purpose Supply chains are essential to economic growth in many industries. However, their complexity and slow response to market changes leave them vulnerable to environmental disruptions. The concept of antifragility explains how organizations can withstand and even thrive during disruptions. The goal of this paper is to review and consolidate the literature on supply chain antifragility and derive a conceptual framework that illustrates how antifragility-oriented capabilities can transform disruptions into long-lasting performance improvements. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature network analysis (SLNA) and a keyword analysis were conducted on articles related to antifragility and supply chain capabilities published in the Scopus database between 2012 and June 2025. Based on the resulting thematic clusters identified through SLNA and keyword analysis, additional literature, and dynamic capability theory, a novel conceptual framework for supply chain antifragility was developed. Findings The SLNA reveals three principal thematic clusters: supply chain vulnerabilities, supply chain enablers, and supply chain capabilities for antifragility. These thematic clusters converge in an integrative conceptual framework showing how antifragility emerges from interactions among disruption drivers and triggers, technological and informational enablers, and antifragility capabilities. These factors collectively facilitate enhanced supply chain antifragility outcomes. Originality/value Introduced in 2012, antifragility offers an alternative perspective to the traditional concepts of robustness and resilience. It has only recently been applied to supply chains, which are subject to common disorder and disruption. By examining the concept in this context and reviewing relevant work, the analyses and conceptual framework developed in this study provide a comprehensive overview, establish a critical foundation for future research, and inform how to take advantage of supply chain antifragility.

title: The Influence Of The Audit Committee, Leverage, Profitability On Tax Aggressiveness With Independent Commissioners As A Moderating Variable
summary: Tax aggressiveness is an action taken by a company to reduce its cost in fulfilling its tax obligations. Companies that engage in tax aggressiveness to save on tax payments will generate higher profits in the future. The purpose of this research is to examine and explain the influence of the audit committee, leverage, profitability, and independent commissioners on the value of manufacturing companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange. The sample size in this study consisted of 107 manufacturing companies from 2021-2023, with 49 outlier data points and a total of 272 companies in the research. Data collection used the non-participant observation method. The data analysis technique used is moderation regression analysis. The analysis results show that the audit committee has a positive and significant effect on tax aggressiveness, leverage has a negative and significant effect on tax aggressiveness, profitability has a positive effect on tax aggressiveness, independent commissioners weaken the influence of the audit committee on tax aggressiveness, independent commissioners weaken the influence of leverage on tax aggressiveness, and independent commissioners strengthen the influence of profitability on tax aggressiveness. The theoretical implication of this research is to provide knowledge and strengthen the theory of corporate agency value related to the audit committee, leverage, profitability, and independent commissioners. The implication of this research is that manufacturing sector companies should be more careful in formulating tax policies that align with the principles of good corporate governance

title: State Control of Labor Logistics and the Structural Impasse of Big Tech: The US Administration's PERM Suspension and the Enclosure of Human Capital Supply Chains
summary: 【Abstract】This strategic systems and institutional economics monograph investigates the systemic fault lines exposed by the United States Department of Labor's suspension of the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program targeting eight major technology conglomerates (including Microsoft, Adobe, and Capgemini). For decades, elite technology incumbents constructed formidable corporate moats through globalized labor arbitrage, cloaking the systematic substitution of domestic engineering talent behind the ideological rhetoric of "borderless innovation" and "hyper-specialized talent shortages." This paper demonstrates that labor migration routes constitute the critical "human physical layer" of high-technology infrastructure. By weaponizing immigration protocols and freezing permanent residency sponsorship channels, the sovereign state has dismantled the performative internationalism of Silicon Valley, asserting direct territorial control over the human capital supply chain. Through a rigorous public-choice and comparative logistics analysis, the monograph reveals how corporate rent-seeking in tech labor markets triggered a direct sovereign counter-intervention, transitioning tech governance from superficial "regulatory theater" to coercive, physical-layer state governance. The paper concludes by presenting a sustainable framework reconciling sovereign labor protection, deterministic supply chain auditing, and Human-in-Command accountability.

title: Rebuilding Big Health Data: An Account of Fifty Studies
summary: Abstract: The uncritical application of legacy statistical machinery to modern Big Health Data has driven a proliferation of clinically unstable and methodologically fragile studies. This review gives an account of the author's extensive research activity over the past year, encompassing a corpus of fifty papers, fifteen of which are fully peer-reviewed, aimed at addressing this methodological crisis despite the widespread and defensive resistance encountered within the academic establishment. By outlining a structured progression from the epistemological auditing of medical artificial intelligence and epidemiological consistency validation to structural dataset auditing and exact finite-count stress testing, this overview suggests that the Big Data Paradox can be solved in the medical field. This passes through the necessity of subordinating massive computational scale to biological plausibility and exact statistical mechanics to safeguard public health informatics.

title: Transformación digital e inteligencia artificial en la gestión agroempresarial: productividad, competitividad y toma de decisiones
summary: La transformación digital y la inteligencia artificial han adquirido relevancia estratégica en la gestión agroempresarial, especialmente por su capacidad para optimizar recursos, mejorar la productividad, fortalecer la competitividad y apoyar decisiones basadas en datos. El objetivo de esta revisión sistemática fue analizar la producción científica reciente sobre la incorporación de tecnologías digitales e inteligencia artificial en la gestión agroempresarial, con énfasis en productividad, competitividad y toma de decisiones. Se desarrolló una revisión sistemática de literatura orientada por PRISMA 2020. La búsqueda se realizó únicamente en Google Scholar, considerando publicaciones entre 2021 y 2026. Se aplicaron criterios de inclusión y exclusión vinculados con pertinencia temática, acceso a texto completo, idioma y relación directa con agricultura digital, IA, gestión agroempresarial, rendimiento productivo, ventaja competitiva o decisiones gerenciales. La muestra final estuvo integrada por 15 estudios, analizados mediante síntesis cualitativa temática. Los resultados evidenciaron cuatro categorías principales: automatización y agricultura inteligente, analítica predictiva y productividad, competitividad agroalimentaria y adopción/gestión de tecnologías digitales. La literatura revisada muestra que la IA y las tecnologías digitales pueden mejorar la eficiencia productiva, la trazabilidad, la planificación, la gestión de riesgos y la toma de decisiones; no obstante, persisten barreras asociadas con infraestructura, costos, capacidades digitales, confianza en los algoritmos, interoperabilidad y brecha digital. Se concluye que la transformación digital agroempresarial requiere estrategias de gestión integradas que combinen tecnología, formación, gobernanza de datos y modelos de adopción inclusivos.
